key_insight: Coccidioidomycosis incidence in Arizona was linked to a layered mix of dust, weather, and especially soil moisture/temperature conditions, suggesting deeper soil environment may matter for disease risk and forecasting.
clinical_relevance: Environmental surveillance that includes subsurface soil conditions may improve outbreak awareness and seasonal prediction of Valley fever in endemic regions.
method: Analyzed 185,486 reported cases from Arizona’s Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties (1997–2024).
Used distributed lag non-linear models to test above-ground and below-ground exposure-lag-response patterns.
Built a two-stage stacked ensemble to compare layer-specific prediction and a combined forecast.
evidence_signal: The study used a large longitudinal surveillance dataset with a strictly held-out test period to evaluate predictive performance across environmental layers.
watch_item: Ecological associations and model performance do not prove causality, and forecasting may not generalize outside Arizona or beyond the available environmental measurements.
paper_title: Effects and predictive performance of multilayer environmental exposures on coccidioidomycosis: a longitudinal surveillance study
